claim: The auditory mismatch negativity (MMN) has been proposed as a biomarker of NMDA receptor (NMDAR) dysfunction in schizophrenia.
source: The auditory mismatch negativity (MMN) has been proposed as a biomarker of NMDA receptor (NMDAR) dysfunction in schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a statement about the proposed use of MMN as a biomarker, supported by references to existing literature in the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: NMDAR dysfunction in schizophrenia may be caused by aberrant interactions of different neuromodulators with NMDARs.
source: Such dysfunction may be caused by aberrant interactions of different neuromodulators with NMDARs, which could explain clinical heterogeneity among patients.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms underlying NMDAR dysfunction.

claim: The muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist biperiden delayed and topographically shifted mismatch responses, particularly during high stability.
source: We found a significant drug × mismatch interaction: while the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist biperiden delayed and topographically shifted mismatch responses, particularly during high stability, this effect could not be detected for amisulpride, a dopamine D2/D3 receptor antagonist.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study showing significant drug × mismatch interaction effects.

claim: Amisulpride, a dopamine D2/D3 receptor antagonist, did not show detectable effects on mismatch responses.
source: We found a significant drug × mismatch interaction: while the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist biperiden delayed and topographically shifted mismatch responses, particularly during high stability, this effect could not be detected for amisulpride, a dopamine D2/D3 receptor antagonist.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of significant effects in the experimental data.

claim: Neither galantamine nor levodopa exerted significant effects on MMN.
source: Neither galantamine nor levodopa, which elevate acetylcholine and dopamine levels, respectively, exerted significant effects on MMN.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant effects of these drugs.

claim: The differential MMN sensitivity to muscarinic versus dopaminergic receptor function may prove useful for developing tests that predict individual treatment responses in schizophrenia.
source: This differential MMN sensitivity to muscarinic versus dopaminergic receptor function may prove useful for developing tests that predict individual treatment responses in schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical applications of the findings.

claim: The auditory MMN is an electrophysiological response to rule violations in auditory input streams.
source: The auditory mismatch negativity (MMN) is an electrophysiological response to rule violations in auditory input streams (Näätänen et al., 2001; Näätänen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: MMN is commonly defined as the difference between event-related potentials (ERPs) to predictable ('standard') and surprising ('deviant') auditory events.
source: It is commonly defined as the difference between event-related potentials (ERPs) to predictable ('standard') and surprising ('deviant') auditory events, and has been interpreted as reflecting the update of a predictive (generative) model of the acoustic environment (Winkler, 2007; Garrido et al., 2009; Lieder et al., 2013a; Lieder et al., 2013b; Weber et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature defining MMN.

claim: MMN has been interpreted as reflecting the update of a predictive (generative) model of the acoustic environment.
source: It is commonly defined as the difference between event-related potentials (ERPs) to predictable ('standard') and surprising ('deviant') auditory events, and has been interpreted as reflecting the update of a predictive (generative) model of the acoustic environment (Winkler, 2007; Garrido et al., 2009; Lieder et al., 2013a; Lieder et al., 2013b; Weber et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical interpretations of MMN.

claim: MMN amplitudes are significantly reduced in patients with schizophrenia.
source: First, there is strong evidence that MMN amplitudes are significantly reduced in patients with schizophrenia (for meta-analyses, see Umbricht and Krljes, 2005; Erickson et al., 2016; Avissar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to meta-analyses showing reduced MMN in schizophrenia patients.

claim: The MMN is sensitive to pharmacological alterations of NMDA receptor (NMDAR) function.
source: Second, numerous studies in animals and humans have demonstrated convincingly that the MMN is sensitive to pharmacological alterations of NMDA receptor (NMDAR) function (Javitt et al., 1996; Umbricht et al., 2000; Heekeren et al., 2008; Schmidt et al., 2012; Rosburg and Kreitschmann-Andermahr, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating NMDAR sensitivity of MMN.

claim: NMDAR function plays a major role in pathophysiological theories of schizophrenia.
source: which, in turn, plays a major role in pathophysiological theories of schizophrenia (Olney and Farber, 1995; Friston, 1998; Goff and Coyle, 2001; Stephan et al., 2006; Stephan et al., 2009; Corlett et al., 2011; Corlett et al., 2016; Javitt, 2012; Friston et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on schizophrenia pathophysiology.

claim: The MMN has been suggested as a potential readout of NMDA receptor (NMDAR) hypofunction in schizophrenia and has been proposed as a promising translational biomarker.
source: The MMN has thus been suggested as a potential readout of NMDA receptor (NMDAR) hypofunction in schizophrenia and has been proposed as a promising translational biomarker (Light and Näätänen, 2013; Todd et al., 2013; Näätänen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature proposing MMN as a biomarker.

claim: After blocking NMDARs with ketamine, the MMN still reflected updates about the regularity in the tone sequence (lower level prediction errors), but updates about the stability of this regularity (higher level PEs) were significantly reduced.
source: We have recently demonstrated that the dependency of the MMN on intact NMDAR signaling can be understood in terms of hierarchical inference about the world's statistical structure (Weber et al., 2020): After blocking NMDARs with ketamine, the MMN still reflected updates about the regularity in the tone sequence (lower level prediction errors, PEs), but updates about the stability of this regularity (higher level PEs) were significantly reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The level of stability in the environment should impact on lower level belief updates by scaling the certainty with which beliefs are held (the precision-weight on the PE).
source: Theoretical accounts (Behrens et al., 2007; Mathys et al., 2011) predict that the level of stability in the environment should impact on lower level belief updates by scaling the certainty with which beliefs are held (the precision-weight on the PE).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical accounts.

claim: The MMN has been found to be sensitive to the overall level of volatility within a block, such that MMN amplitudes were higher in blocks with more stable regularities.
source: Consistent with this, the MMN has previously also been found to be sensitive to the overall level of volatility within a block, such that MMN amplitudes were higher in blocks with more stable regularities (Todd et al., 2014; Dzafic et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing volatility effects on MMN.

claim: Acetylcholine (ACh) and dopamine (DA) are two modulatory transmitters with a general capacity to modulate NMDAR function.
source: Acetylcholine (ACh) and dopamine (DA) are two modulatory transmitters with a general capacity to modulate NMDAR function (Hallett et al., 2006; Lin et al., 2010; Zappettini et al., 2014; Zwart et al., 2018; for review, see Gu, 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing ACh and DA modulation of NMDARs.

claim: The relative contribution of ACh and DA to NMDAR dysregulation has been suggested as a major cause of heterogeneity in clinical trajectories among patients with schizophrenia.
source: and their relative contribution to NMDAR dysregulation has been suggested as a major cause of heterogeneity in clinical trajectories among patients with schizophrenia ('dysconnection hypothesis', Stephan et al., 2006; Stephan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the dysconnection hypothesis.

claim: Some of the most potent antipsychotics (olanzapine and clozapine) have strong affinity to cholinergic (specifically: muscarinic) receptors, in contrast to almost all other second generation antipsychotics.
source: Most notably, some of the most potent antipsychotics (olanzapine and clozapine) have strong affinity to cholinergic (specifically: muscarinic) receptors (Lavalaye et al., 2001), in contrast to almost all other second generation antipsychotics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on antipsychotic receptor binding profiles.

claim: Nicotinic stimulation has been demonstrated to enhance MMN amplitudes.
source: While nicotinic stimulation has been demonstrated to enhance MMN amplitudes (Harkrider and Hedrick, 2005; Inami et al., 2005; Inami et al., 2007; Baldeweg et al., 2006; Dunbar et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2009; Fisher et al., 2012; Knott et al., 2012; Hamilton et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing nicotinic enhancement of MMN.

claim: The role of muscarinic cholinergic receptors for MMN is less well established.
source: the role of muscarinic cholinergic receptors for MMN is less well established.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The few human studies investigating the effects of muscarinic antagonists scopolamine and biperiden on auditory mismatch processing were inconclusive and showed mixed results.
source: The few human studies investigating the effects of muscarinic antagonists scopolamine and biperiden on auditory mismatch processing were inconclusive and showed mixed results (Pekkonen et al., 2001; Pekkonen et al., 2005; Klinkenberg et al., 2013; Caldenhove et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies with mixed results.

claim: Several pharmacological studies of DA failed to show significant effects on MMN.
source: Similarly, while several pharmacological studies of DA failed to show significant effects on MMN (Kähkönen et al., 2002; Leung et al., 2007; Leung et al., 2010; Korostenskaja et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing no DA effects on MMN.

claim: Some studies reported significant alterations of MMN by antipsychotic drug treatment, hinting at a possible effect of DA.
source: other studies reported significant alterations of MMN by antipsychotic drug treatment, hinting at a possible effect of DA (Kähkönen et al., 2001; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing antipsychotic effects on MMN.

claim: In study 1 (N = 81), the effects of biperiden, a selective muscarinic M1 receptor antagonist, on mismatch related ERPs were tested and compared to the effects of amisulpride, a selective dopaminergic D2/3 receptor antagonist.
source: In study 1 (N = 81), we tested the effects of biperiden, a selective muscarinic M1 receptor antagonist, on mismatch related ERPs, and compare them to the effects of amisulpride, a selective dopaminergic D2/3 receptor antagonist.
evidence: This is a description of the study design.

claim: In study 2, the same study design, paradigm, and analysis strategy were employed in a separate sample (N = 81) to test the impact of elevated cholinergic vs. dopaminergic transmission on mismatch amplitudes, contrasting the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor galantamine to the dopamine precursor levodopa.
source: In study 2, we employed exactly the same study design, paradigm, and analysis strategy in a separate sample (N = 81), to test the impact of elevated cholinergic vs. dopaminergic transmission on mismatch amplitudes, contrasting the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor galantamine to the dopamine precursor levodopa.
evidence: This is a description of the study design.

claim: Estimates of the actual drug plasma levels at the time participants performed the experimental task were used to account for individual differences in pharmacokinetics.
source: In both studies, we used estimates of the actual drug plasma levels at the time participants performed the experimental task in order to account for individual differences in pharmacokinetics.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach.

claim: A new variant of an auditory oddball paradigm with explicitly varying levels of stability over time was used.
source: Importantly, we used a new variant of an auditory oddball paradigm with explicitly varying levels of stability over time.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental paradigm.

claim: Volatility affects precision-weighting of prediction error responses, possibly via interactions of ACh and NMDA-receptor-dependent mechanisms.
source: This was motivated by theoretical accounts (Mathys et al., 2011) and experimental findings that volatility affects precision-weighting of prediction error responses, possibly via interactions of ACh and NMDA-receptor-dependent mechanisms (Iglesias et al., 2013; Weber et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Mismatch responses are expected to be sensitive to volatility, with larger mismatch amplitudes during more stable phases.
source: Based on previous literature, one would expect mismatch responses in our paradigm to be sensitive to (1) volatility, with larger mismatch amplitudes during more stable phases (Todd et al., 2014; Dzafic et al., 2020; Weber et al., 2020)
evidence: This is a prediction based on citations to previous literature.

claim: Galantamine is expected to increase and biperiden to reduce mismatch amplitudes based on cholinergic manipulations.
source: and (2) cholinergic manipulations, with galantamine increasing and biperiden reducing mismatch amplitudes (Moran et al., 2013; Schöbi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a prediction based on citations to previous literature.

claim: A differential effect of cholinergic (muscarinic) and dopaminergic receptor status on mismatch responses was expected.
source: Furthermore, we expected (3) a differential effect of cholinergic (muscarinic) and dopaminergic receptor status on mismatch responses, as postulated by initial work on MMN-based computational assays (Stephan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a prediction based on citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: Muscarinic receptors play a critical role for the generation of mismatch responses and their dependence on environmental volatility.
source: Our results suggest that muscarinic receptors play a critical role for the generation of mismatch responses and their dependence on environmental volatility, whereas no such evidence was found for dopamine receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: No evidence was found for dopamine receptors playing a critical role in the generation of mismatch responses and their dependence on environmental volatility.
source: Our results suggest that muscarinic receptors play a critical role for the generation of mismatch responses and their dependence on environmental volatility, whereas no such evidence was found for dopamine receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing absence of effects.

claim: In study 1, after data exclusion, N = 71 datasets entered the group analyses (placebo: N = 25, amisulpride: N = 24, biperiden: N = 22).
source: After data exclusion, N = 71 datasets entered the group analyses for study 1 (placebo: N = 25, amisulpride: N = 24, biperiden: N = 22)
evidence: This is a factual statement about the sample size after exclusions.

claim: In study 2, N = 78 datasets entered the group analyses (N = 26 per group).
source: and N = 78 for study 2 (N = 26 per group).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the sample size.

claim: All steps of the analysis pipeline, including data exclusion criteria and statistical contrasts of interest, were specified in a time-stamped analysis plan prior to the unblinding of the researcher conducting the analysis.
source: All steps of our analysis pipeline, including data exclusion criteria and statistical contrasts of interest, were specified in a time-stamped analysis plan prior to the unblinding of the researcher conducting the analysis (see Materials and Methods, section Analysis plan, data and code availability).
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological approach to ensure rigor.

claim: Participants passively listened to a sequence of 1800 tones while performing a visual distraction task.
source: Participants passively listened to a sequence of 1800 tones while performing a visual distraction task.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task, also shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Visual events occurred after tone presentations at a randomly varying delay between 50 and 250 ms after tone offset, in 36 (study 1) and 90 (study 2) out of 1800 trials.
source: Visual events occurred after tone presentations at a randomly varying delay between 50 and 250 ms after tone offset, in 36 (study 1) and 90 (study 2) out of 1800 trials.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design, also illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Participants reacted to visual targets on average after 509.8 ms (SD = 72.6) in study 1 and 460.4 ms (SD = 54.2) in study 2.
source: Participants reacted to visual targets on average after 509.8 ms (SD = 72.6; study 1) and 460.4 ms (SD = 54.2; study 2)
evidence: This is a factual statement about behavioral data.

claim: Participants responded correctly to 94.8% (SD = 7.0) of the presented targets in study 1 and 95.6% (SD = 5.3) in study 2.
source: and responded correctly to 94.8% (SD = 7.0; study 1) and 95.6% (SD = 5.3; study 2) of the presented targets.
evidence: This is a factual statement about behavioral data.

claim: There were no significant differences between drug groups in their performance on the visual distraction task in study 1.
source: There were no significant differences between drug groups in their performance in study 1, as assessed with a one-way ANOVA for reaction times (F = 1.32, p = 0.27) and a Kruskal Wallis test for hit rates (χ2 = 2.92, p = 0.23, Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical tests on behavioral data, also shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In study 2, reaction times did not differ significantly between drug groups.
source: In study 2, reaction times again did not differ significantly between drug groups (ANOVA F = 0.55, p = 0.58)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical tests on behavioral data.

claim: In study 2, there was a significant effect of drug group on hit rates.
source: but there was a significant effect of drug group on hit rates (Kruskal-Wallis χ2 = 8.36, p = 0.01, Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical tests on behavioral data, also shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hit rates in the galantamine group were significantly higher than in the levodopa group in study 2.
source: Post-hoc pairwise comparisons indicated that hit rates in the galantamine group were significantly higher than in the levodopa group (p = 0.019; the difference to the placebo group failed to reach significance: p = 0.06).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical comparisons.

claim: Mismatch effects were different between drug groups in study 1: biperiden delayed and topographically shifted mismatch signals compared to amisulpride and placebo.
source: In study 1, mismatch effects were different between drug groups: biperiden delayed and topographically shifted mismatch signals compared to amisulpride and placebo (see Figure 2A for selected sensors, and Figure 2B for selected time points).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and visualized in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Between 160 ms and 172 ms after tone onset, the difference between standard and deviant ERPs was significantly smaller in the biperiden group compared to the amisulpride group at pre-frontal sensors, peaking at 164 ms (t = 4.45, p = 0.012).
source: When considering the whole time × sensor space and correcting for multiple comparisons using Gaussian random field (GRF) theory, this difference was significant at pre-frontal sensors for the comparison between the amisulpride and the biperiden group: between 160 ms and 172 ms after tone onset, the difference between standard and deviant ERPs was significantly smaller in the biperiden group compared to the amisulpride group, peaking at 164 ms (t = 4.45, p = 0.012, Figure 2C, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data, shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: In study 2, there were no significant differences in mismatch ERPs between drug groups.
source: In study 2, there were no significant differences in mismatch ERPs between drug groups, both when considering the whole time × sensor space and when constraining the search volume to the significant average mismatch effect using the functionally defined mask.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of significant effects in statistical analysis.

claim: ERPs to deviants were significantly different from ERPs to standards in large parts of the time × sensor space in study 1, including the classical mismatch negativity in fronto-central channels between 100 and 250 ms after tone onset.
source: ERPs to deviants were significantly different from ERPs to standards in large parts of the time × sensor space, including the classical mismatch negativity in fronto-central channels between 100 and 250 ms after tone onset.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In a large cluster of frontal, fronto-central, and central sensors, ERPs to standard tones were significantly more positive than ERPs to deviant tones from 100 to 232 ms after tone onset, with a peak difference at 172 ms (t = 16.59, p < 0.001) in study 1.
source: in a large cluster of frontal, fronto-central, and central sensors, ERPs to standard tones were significantly more positive than ERPs to deviant tones from 100 to 232 ms after tone onset, with a peak difference at 172 ms (t = 16.59, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data.

claim: In study 1, mismatch was significantly stronger in stable as compared to volatile phases between 180 and 220 ms after tone onset, with a peak difference at 204 ms (t = 5.13, p = 0.001) at central and centro-parietal sensors.
source: In study 1, we found such an interaction effect (mismatch × stability) in 3 clusters. Between 180 and 220 ms after tone onset, mismatch was significantly stronger in stable as compared to volatile phases, with a peak difference at 204 ms (t = 5.13, p = 0.001) at central and centro-parietal sensors.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data showing interaction effects.

claim: In study 2, ERPs showed no significant interaction effects between the factors mismatch and stability.
source: In study 2, ERPs showed no significant interaction effects between the factors mismatch and stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of significant effects in statistical analysis.

claim: The interaction effect between mismatch and stability was significant only in the biperiden group (208 ms, t = 4.96, p = 0.009) at right central channels, but not in the placebo or the amisulpride group.
source: Indeed, when examining the drug groups separately, the interaction effect was significant only in the biperiden group (208 ms, t = 4.96, p = 0.009) at right central channels, but not in the placebo or the amisulpride group.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data in separate drug groups.

claim: The interaction of mismatch and stability was stronger in the biperiden group compared to the placebo group at 212 ms at right central sensors (t = 3.18, p = 0.034 after small volume correction).
source: However, focusing on only those parts of the time × sensor space where there was a significant positive interaction between mismatch and stability (cluster 1 in Table 4), we did find a significant three-way interaction such that the interaction of mismatch and stability was stronger in the biperiden group compared to the placebo group at 212 ms at right central sensors (t = 3.18, p = 0.034 after small volume correction, see Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis with small volume correction, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Drug groups differed significantly in their mismatch response during stable periods in study 1.
source: Indeed, while there were no significant effects of drug group on mismatch in volatile phases, drug groups did differ significantly in their mismatch response during stable periods.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data during stable phases.

claim: Pre-frontal sensors showed significantly reduced mismatch responses between 160 ms and 168 ms after tone onset in the biperiden group compared to the amisulpride group during stable periods, peaking at 164ms (t = 4.74, p = 0.016).
source: Again, as for overall mismatch, pre-frontal sensors showed significantly reduced mismatch responses between 160 ms and 168 ms after tone onset in the biperiden group compared to the amisulpride group, peaking at 164ms (t = 4.74, p = 0.016).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data during stable phases.

claim: Later mismatch responses were significantly larger in the biperiden group compared to placebo at right central and centro-parietal sensors during stable periods.
source: Additionally, later mismatch responses were significantly larger in the biperiden group compared to placebo at right central and centro-parietal sensors (see Table 5 and Figure 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of ERP data during stable phases, shown in Table 5 and Figure 2D.

claim: In study 2, the three drug groups did not differ in how mismatch ERPs were affected by the stability of the current context.
source: In study 2, the three drug groups did not differ in how mismatch ERPs were affected by the stability of the current context (three-way interaction with factor drug).
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of significant three-way interaction effects.

claim: Biperiden, a selective muscarinic (cholinergic) M1 receptor antagonist, delays and topographically shifts mismatch responses in the auditory oddball paradigm.
source: In study 1, we found that biperiden, a selective muscarinic (cholinergic) M1 receptor antagonist, delays and topographically shifts mismatch responses in this paradigm
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Inhibiting dopaminergic D2/3 receptor transmission by administration of amisulpride did not produce the effect observed with biperiden.
source: while we did not observe this effect when inhibiting dopaminergic D2/3 receptor transmission by administration of amisulpride.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data showing absence of effects.

claim: Neither elevated cholinergic nor dopaminergic transmission, as induced in study 2 by galantamine and levodopa, respectively, resulted in observable changes to deviance processing in the task.
source: Neither elevated cholinergic nor dopaminergic transmission, as induced in study 2 by galantamine and levodopa, respectively, resulted in observable changes to deviance processing in our task.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data showing absence of effects.

claim: Antagonizing muscarinic cholinergic receptors with biperiden affected deviance processing particularly during stable phases of the task along with a significant interaction between deviance and stability.
source: We found that antagonizing muscarinic cholinergic receptors with biperiden affected deviance processing particularly during stable phases of our task along with a significant interaction between deviance and stability.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: In study 1, mismatch responses in the biperiden group peaked later and were distributed more towards right centro-parietal channels than in the other drug groups.
source: In study 1, mismatch responses in the biperiden group peaked later and were distributed more towards right centro-parietal channels than in the other drug groups (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings, visualized in Figure 2B.

claim: The biperiden-induced shift resulted in significantly smaller mismatch amplitudes at pre-frontal sensors early on, in classical MMN time windows (biperiden vs. amisulpride), and significantly larger MMN at centro-parietal sensors later (biperiden vs. placebo).
source: This resulted in significantly smaller mismatch amplitudes at pre-frontal sensors early on, in classical MMN time windows (biperiden vs. amisulpride), and significantly larger MMN at centro-parietal sensors later (biperiden vs. placebo).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Effects of cholinergic agents on MMN have been demonstrated repeatedly, mostly showing enhanced mismatch amplitudes or shortened MMN latencies in response to stimulation of nicotinic cholinergic receptors.
source: Effects of cholinergic agents on MMN have been demonstrated repeatedly, mostly showing enhanced mismatch amplitudes or shortened MMN latencies in response to stimulation of nicotinic cholinergic receptors (Baldeweg et al., 2004; Harkrider and Hedrick, 2005; Dunbar et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2009; Knott et al., 2012; Hamilton et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Previous investigations of the effects of antagonizing muscarinic cholinergic receptors have yielded less consistent results.
source: In contrast, previous investigations of the effects of antagonizing muscarinic cholinergic receptors have yielded less consistent results.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Studies using the muscarinic antagonist scopolamine have reported reductions of MMN amplitudes, no effects on MMN, and reduced P300 responses to targets in active oddball tasks.
source: Studies using the muscarinic antagonist scopolamine have reported reductions of MMN amplitudes (Pekkonen et al., 2001), no effects on MMN (Pekkonen et al., 2005), and reduced P300 responses to targets in active oddball tasks (Meador et al., 1989; Curran et al., 1998; Brown et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies with varied results.

claim: Biperiden has about tenfold higher affinity for M1 as compared to M2–M5 receptors.
source: Biperiden differs from scopolamine in the specificity of its binding affinity: it has about tenfold higher affinity for M1 as compared to M2–M5 receptors (Bolden et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on receptor binding affinity.

claim: Two studies have tested the effects of biperiden on deviance detection in passive auditory oddball tasks and neither study found effects on MMN, but hints of a potential effect on P3a amplitudes.
source: Two studies have tested the effects of biperiden on deviance detection in passive auditory oddball tasks (Klinkenberg et al., 2013; Caldenhove et al., 2017). Neither study found effects on MMN, but hints of a potential effect on P3a amplitudes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both previous biperiden studies used only half the dose (2 mg) of biperiden as administered in the current study, which might explain the difference in findings.
source: Importantly, both previous studies used only half the dose (2 mg) of biperiden as administered here, which might explain the difference in findings compared to our study.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between studies.

claim: The current study provides a characterization of the drug effect on mismatch responses across the full time × sensor space, while correcting for multiple comparisons across time and sensors.
source: Here, we provide a characterization of the drug effect on mismatch responses across the full time × sensor space, while correcting for multiple comparisons across time and sensors.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach.

claim: The biperiden-induced shift affects traditional MMN sensors (Fz, FCz, Cz) less than those at the border of the MMN scalp distribution (Fp1, Fp2, C2, C4), which is where significant effects of biperiden were found.
source: Importantly, this shift affects traditional MMN sensors (Fz, FCz, Cz), which have mostly been examined in previous studies, less than those at the border of the MMN scalp distribution (Fp1, Fp2, C2, C4), which is where we found significant effects of biperiden.
evidence: This is an observation about the spatial distribution of effects.

claim: The use of individual drug plasma level estimates in the group level GLM, based on the analysis of blood samples, allowed accounting for interindividual differences in pharmacokinetics.
source: Another strength of our study design – with total N = 162 across studies – was the use of individual drug plasma level estimates in the group level GLM, based on the analysis of blood samples, which allowed us to account for interindividual differences in pharmacokinetics.
evidence: This is a description of a methodological strength.

claim: The focus on male participants was intended to avoid confounds of fluctuating estrogen levels, which have been found to significantly impact on dopaminergic and cholinergic systems.
source: The focus on male participants was intended to avoid confounds of fluctuating estrogen levels, which have been found to significantly impact on dopaminergic and cholinergic systems (Gasbarri et al., 2012; Colzato and Hommel, 2014; Barth et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a justification for the study design, supported by citations.

claim: The focus on male participants constitutes a significant limitation of the study, as it means that the results may not equally apply to both sexes.
source: However, this also constitutes a significant limitation of our study, as it means that our results may not equally apply to both sexes and will therefore need to be replicated in a more representative sample in future work.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: In study 2, no effect of galantamine on mismatch responses was found, in contrast to a previous report showing an augmentation of MMN under the same dose of galantamine.
source: Surprisingly, in study 2, we did not find an effect of galantamine on mismatch responses. This is in contrast to a previous report showing an augmentation of MMN under the same dose of galantamine as administered here (Moran et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with previous literature.

claim: The study by Moran and colleagues employed a 'roving' oddball paradigm where a tone sequence comprised mini-blocks of 6–10 tone repetitions, where consecutive mini-blocks differed in frequency, and the first tone of a block represented the deviant.
source: The study by Moran and colleagues employed a 'roving' oddball paradigm (Garrido et al., 2008): a tone sequence comprised mini-blocks of 6–10 tone repetitions, where consecutive mini-blocks differed in frequency, and the first tone of a block represented the deviant.
evidence: This is a description of the paradigm used in a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: In the current paradigm, mini-blocks of repeated tones tended to be much shorter than in the Moran study (less than 20% of mini-blocks with 6 repetitions or more, more than 60% consisting of 2 repetitions or less), making the paradigm considerably more volatile overall.
source: In contrast, in our paradigm, mini-blocks of repeated tones tended to be much shorter (less than 20% of mini-blocks with 6 repetitions or more, more than 60% consisting of 2 repetitions or less), making our paradigm considerably more volatile overall.
evidence: This is a comparison of paradigm characteristics.

claim: The comparably high tonic volatility in the current paradigm could mean that precision-weights on PEs were already high, which might have prevented any increase in sensory precision afforded by galantamine to be expressed in the mismatch ERPs due to a ceiling effect.
source: Speculatively, this comparably high tonic volatility could mean that precision-weights on PEs were already high; this might have prevented any increase in sensory precision afforded by galantamine to be expressed in the mismatch ERPs in our study due to a ceiling effect.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the absence of galantamine effects.

claim: The analysis differed from previous investigations of the effects of biperiden and galantamine on the MMN in terms of pre-processing choices such as the choice of reference, the amount of high-pass filtering and the application of baseline correction.
source: Notably, our analysis differed from previous investigations of the effects of biperiden and galantamine on the MMN (e.g. Klinkenberg et al., 2013; Moran et al., 2013; Caldenhove et al., 2017) in terms of pre-processing choices such as the choice of reference, the amount of high-pass filtering and the application of baseline correction.
evidence: This is a description of methodological differences between studies.

claim: When adopting the adapted pipeline with settings equivalent to previous reports, significant effects of biperiden (versus placebo and amisulpride) on mismatch signals were found that were compatible with an increase in MMN latency.
source: The results of this analysis were largely supportive of our claims: we also found significant effects of biperiden (versus placebo and amisulpride) on mismatch signals that were compatible with an increase in MMN latency, even when adopting the same pipeline as used in previous studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by results from control analyses using alternative preprocessing.

claim: There was still no effect of galantamine on mismatch responses in a whole time × sensor space analysis based on the adapted pipeline.
source: Similarly, there was still no effect of galantamine on mismatch responses in a whole time × sensor space analysis based on this adapted pipeline.
evidence: This claim is supported by results from control analyses showing absence of effects.

claim: In classical oddball paradigms, the occasional deviant represents a rule violation, but its impact on subsequent rule representation is limited, as the tone sequence reverts back to the standard tone immediately.
source: In classical oddball paradigms, the occasional deviant represents a rule violation, but its impact on subsequent rule representation is limited, as the tone sequence reverts back to the standard tone immediately.
evidence: This is a description of classical oddball paradigms based on established knowledge.

claim: In the roving oddball paradigm, every deviant signals the onset of a new rule, examining model updating in a changing environment.
source: In contrast, the roving oddball paradigm examines model updating in a changing environment, as every deviant signals the onset of a new rule.
evidence: This is a description of the roving oddball paradigm based on established knowledge.

claim: In the new volatility oddball paradigm, the relevance of the detected rule violation to the representation of the rule additionally varies across different periods of the experiment.
source: In our new volatility oddball paradigm, the relevance of the detected rule violation to the representation of the rule additionally varies across different periods of the experiment
evidence: This is a description of the novel paradigm design.

claim: During more stable phases, oddballs represent noise and deviants should not lead to a major update of the current belief about the underlying rule.
source: during more stable phases, oddballs represent noise and deviants should not lead to a major update of the current belief about the underlying rule.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about behavior in the paradigm.

claim: During volatile phases, the probabilities of the two tones sometimes reverse and deviants thus occasionally signal the onset of a new rule.
source: In contrast, during volatile phases, the probabilities of the two tones sometimes reverse and deviants thus occasionally signal the onset of a new rule.
evidence: This is a description of the paradigm design.

claim: Theoretical treatments suggest that volatility can impact on the size of belief updates in two opposing ways: increased belief uncertainty due to environmental volatility should increase learning rates, while stable phases allow for a more precise prediction of the input.
source: Theoretical treatments suggest that this volatility can impact on the size of belief updates in two opposing ways (Mathys et al., 2011). On the one hand, increased belief uncertainty due to environmental volatility should increase learning rates (i.e., belief updates) – in other words, deviants are more meaningful in volatile phases due to the occasional rule switch. On the other hand, stable phases allow for a more precise prediction of the input than volatile phases, as beliefs about the more likely tone occurrence are allowed to accumulate for longer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: In study 1, a significant difference between stable and volatile mismatch responses was found, such that mismatch was stronger in stable than in volatile periods, mirroring previous reports of volatility effects on mismatch signals.
source: In study 1, we found a significant difference between stable and volatile mismatch responses, such that mismatch was stronger in stable than in volatile periods (Figure 3). This mirrored previous reports of volatility effects on mismatch signals (Todd et al., 2014; Dzafic et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous literature, shown in Figure 3.

claim: The volatility effect on mismatch in study 1 was mainly due to the altered mismatch response in the biperiden group.
source: However, in our study, this was mainly due to the altered mismatch response in the biperiden group
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of results across drug groups.

claim: Neither the placebo group nor the amisulpride group showed interaction effects between mismatch and stability on their own.
source: Neither the placebo group nor the amisulpride group showed interaction effects on their own
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of significant effects in these groups.

claim: Previous reports have presented effects of block-wise volatility changes on mismatch processing in single-channel analyses, and the whole-volume corrected effect did not replicate in a validation data set, suggesting that the effects of block-wise volatility on mismatch might be relatively subtle.
source: It should also be noted that previous reports have presented effects of block-wise volatility changes on mismatch processing in single-channel analyses (focusing only on Fz, Todd et al., 2014; Dzafic et al., 2020), and that the whole-volume corrected effect presented in Dzafic et al., 2020 did not replicate in a validation data set, suggesting that the effects of block-wise volatility on mismatch might be relatively subtle compared to the size of the mismatch effect itself (and thus require more aggressive pre-processing or higher trial numbers to be robustly detected).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and their replication attempts.

claim: Trial-wise EEG amplitudes of the classical MMN component correlated with lower-level prediction errors about tone probabilities, while later P3-like components scaled with a higher-level prediction error about environmental volatility.
source: in that we found multiple, hierarchically related prediction errors underlying EEG mismatch signals: trial-wise EEG amplitudes of the classical MMN component correlated with lower-level prediction errors about tone probabilities, while later P3-like components scaled with a higher-level prediction error about environmental volatility.
evidence: This claim is supported by model-based analysis results presented in Appendix 1.

claim: Only biperiden affected the EEG signatures of model-derived precision-weighted prediction errors – neither dopaminergic manipulations nor galantamine showed significant differences to the placebo group.
source: Importantly, in line with the results from the conventional averaging approach, we found that only biperiden affected the EEG signatures of model-derived precision-weighted prediction errors – neither dopaminergic manipulations nor galantamine showed significant differences to the placebo group.
evidence: This claim is supported by model-based analysis results.

claim: The biperiden effect concerned not only signatures of low-level prediction errors, reflecting mismatches between expected and actual tone identities, but also signatures of higher level prediction errors serving to refine beliefs about environmental volatility.
source: Moreover, the biperiden effect concerned not only signatures of low-level prediction errors, reflecting mismatches between expected and actual tone identities, but also signatures of higher level prediction errors serving to refine beliefs about environmental volatility.
evidence: This claim is supported by model-based analysis results.

claim: Mismatch responses in the auditory oddball paradigm were sensitive to muscarinic receptor status.
source: Together, the current analyses demonstrate that mismatch responses in our paradigm were sensitive to muscarinic receptor status.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Dopaminergic challenges in both studies did not affect mismatch responses, in line with previous reports.
source: In contrast, and in line with previous reports (Kähkönen et al., 2002; Leung et al., 2007; Leung et al., 2010; Korostenskaja et al., 2008), dopaminergic challenges in both of our studies did not affect mismatch responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Such a differential sensitivity to cholinergic versus dopaminergic neuromodulation may prove valuable for understanding and predicting differential treatment responses in individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia.
source: Such a differential sensitivity to cholinergic versus dopaminergic neuromodulation may prove valuable for understanding and predicting differential treatment responses in individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical applications.

claim: While the reduction of MMN amplitudes in patients compared to healthy controls is robust and of large effect size, there is still considerable inter-individual variation in MMN amplitudes among patients.
source: Importantly, while the reduction of MMN amplitudes in patients compared to healthy controls is robust and of large effect size (Erickson et al., 2016), there is still considerable inter-individual variation in MMN amplitudes among patients (Light and Swerdlow, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on MMN in schizophrenia patients.

claim: Reduced MMN in patients might be relatively more indicative of cholinergic versus dopaminergic dysregulation of synaptic plasticity.
source: Based on our results, we speculate that reduced MMN in patients might be relatively more indicative of cholinergic versus dopaminergic dysregulation of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the experimental findings.

claim: There is compelling evidence for a subgroup of patients with markedly decreased M1 receptor availability in the prefrontal cortex.
source: Notably, there is compelling evidence for a subgroup of patients with markedly decreased M1 receptor availability in the prefrontal cortex (Scarr et al., 2009, see also Gibbons et al., 2013 and Scarr et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on M1 receptor availability in patients.

claim: A key pathophysiological dimension of the heterogeneity of schizophrenia may derive from differential impairment of cholinergic versus dopaminergic modulation of NMDAR function.
source: This is consistent with the possibility that a key pathophysiological dimension of the heterogeneity of schizophrenia derives from differential impairment of cholinergic versus dopaminergic modulation of NMDAR function (Stephan et al., 2006; Stephan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on schizophrenia heterogeneity.

claim: Some of the most effective neuroleptic drugs (e.g., clozapine, olanzapine) differ from other atypical antipsychotics (e.g., amisulpride) in their binding affinity to muscarinic cholinergic receptors.
source: Distinguishing these potential subtypes of schizophrenia could be highly relevant for treatment selection, as some of the most effective neuroleptic drugs (e.g., clozapine, olanzapine) differ from other atypical antipsychotics (e.g., amisulpride) in their binding affinity to muscarinic cholinergic receptors.
evidence: This is a statement about pharmacological properties of antipsychotic drugs based on established knowledge.

claim: The exact mechanisms by which muscarinic receptors are involved in the therapeutic effects of clozapine and olanzapine are still under debate.
source: The exact mechanisms by which muscarinic receptors are involved in the therapeutic effects of clozapine and olanzapine are still under debate
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Proposed mechanisms for muscarinic involvement in clozapine and olanzapine effects include elevation of extracellular levels of acetylcholine in cortex, possibly via blocking presynaptic muscarinic autoreceptors, and normalization of M1 receptor availability in cortex.
source: and include, for example, elevation of extracellular levels of acetylcholine in cortex (Ichikawa et al., 2002; Shirazi-Southall et al., 2002; Weiner et al., 2004), possibly via blocking presynaptic muscarinic autoreceptors (see Johnson et al., 2005; Tzavara et al., 2006 for conflicting data), and normalization of M1 receptor availability in cortex (Malkoff et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on mechanisms of antipsychotic action.

claim: Muscarinic receptors have become an important target of drug development for schizophrenia.
source: Indeed, muscarinic receptors have become an important target of drug development for schizophrenia (Yohn and Conn, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review on drug development.

claim: Previous studies have shown promising results for the MMN, with high intra-class correlation coefficients (up to > 0.90) and other stability measures in both healthy and clinical populations.
source: Generally, previous studies have shown promising results for the MMN, with high intra-class correlation coefficients (up to > 0.90) and other stability measures in both healthy and clinical populations (Light et al., 2012; Roach et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to test-retest reliability studies.

claim: ERPs tend to be idiosyncratic in their expression, but reliable within individuals.
source: consistent with the idea that ERPs tend to be idiosyncratic in their expression, but reliable within individuals (Gaspar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on ERP reliability.

claim: A dedicated test-retest reliability study for the specific MMN variant in this article has not yet been conducted.
source: However, a dedicated test-retest reliability study for the specific MMN variant in this article has not yet been conducted.
evidence: This is a statement about what has not been done.

claim: Prospective patient studies are needed to test whether the readout of cholinergic neurotransmission is predictive of treatment success in individual patients.
source: Second, prospective patient studies are needed, which test whether this readout of cholinergic neurotransmission is predictive of treatment success in individual patients.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The 'generative embedding' strategy involves estimating synaptic variables of (generative) neuronal circuit models of MMN and using these estimates as features for subsequent machine learning.
source: In particular, such a prediction may become possible by adopting the 'generative embedding' strategy frequently used in translational neuromodeling and computational psychiatry (Stephan et al., 2017): this involves estimating synaptic variables of (generative) neuronal circuit models of MMN and using these estimates as features for subsequent machine learning.
evidence: This is a description of a computational approach, supported by citation.

claim: The potential of the computational 'generative embedding' strategy, in the specific context of muscarinic manipulations of the MMN, was demonstrated by a recent rodent study.
source: While the potential of this computational strategy, in the specific context of muscarinic manipulations of the MMN, was demonstrated by a recent rodent study (Schöbi et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a rodent study.

claim: An important question for future work is whether the generative embedding strategy can be successfully translated to a clinical setting.
source: an important question for future work is whether it can be successfully translated to a clinical setting.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.
